Cases Deaths Hospitalizations Vaccines Variants Wastewater Data About More resources More COVID-19 Cases, %%COUNTRY%% WHO will utilize various sources to continue monitoring the COVID-19 epidemiological situation via the WHO COVID-19 dashboard. If data for certain countries is unavailable in this section, it may indicate that they have either ceased reporting COVID-19 surveillance data to WHO or have integrated the COVID-19 surveillance into existing respiratory disease surveillance. In the latter case, SARS-CoV-2 detections from sentinel and systematic virological surveillance sites in those countries may be found in the Circulation section which also includes information on SARS-CoV-2 variant circulation. This global summary of COVID-19 cases includes data on confirmed cases reported to WHO from the comprehensive COVID-19 case monitoring. Coronavirus (COVID-19) cases, %%COUNTRY%% data Source: World Health Organization Loading... Loading... Loading... What is the definition of 'confirmed' and 'reported' in COVID-19 data? All data represents the date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. In the context of WHO's statistical reporting of COVID-19 data, it is important to note that only confirmed cases are included in case and death counts. In guidance updated on 22 July 2023; there are two alternative definitions for 'Confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection' in international surveillance reporting, although some departures may exist due to local adaptations: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria OR epidemiological criteria. b) A person meeting clinical criteria AND/OR epidemiological criteria (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. Additionally, WHO only disseminates data as reported by its Member States. From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data has been compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported directly to WHO headquarters by Member States. Statistical counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these statistics at a global level. Please note that statistics do not necessarily reflect the actual number of cases and deaths or the actual number of countries where cases and deaths are occurring, as a number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting. Trends in COVID-19 cases, %%COUNTRY%% Recent COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, July 2023 - present Source: World Health Organization Data may be incomplete for the latest week. Total COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, January 2020 - present Source: World Health Organization Why is COVID-19 data being presented as weekly statistics? A number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting COVID-19 case and death counts to WHO. An outcome of these differences in reporting is that WHO may receive daily data from some countries, while other countries may only report data to WHO once every 14 days. In addition, countries differ in how they choose to report statistics; some countries provide their data attributed to specific dates while others who report less frequently may group data from 7 days into a single statistic attributed to a week in their reporting. As of 25 August 2023, WHO declared that it is no longer necessary for Member States to report daily counts of cases and deaths to WHO and requested strengthening of weekly reporting. Reported data is still available attributed to specific dates (daily data) here as a download. This dashboard presents the same statistics as weekly figures in charts in order to mitigate against the visual misinterpretation of data. Should daily data have been presented here, many countries would show zero counts for multiple consecutive days due in part to the differences in how they choose to report. While weekly intervals do not completely mitigate against this, the approach reduces the risk that some dashboard users might infer zero cases or deaths when lack of data is often due to reporting differences. What do negative counts of cases or deaths mean? All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected by Member States at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections in their reporting. Bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. Aggregate groups (weekly data to week end date) Source: World Health Organization COVID-19 cases, country level trends Percent change based on previous 28 days Source: World Health Organization Metadata Glossary and definitions Confirmed COVID-19 case Although COVID-19 defines the symptomatic disease caused by SARS-CoV-2, the cases are presented in this dashboard meet one of two alternate definitions of confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection in international surveillance reporting: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria* OR epidemiological criteria*. b) A person meeting clinical criteria* AND/OR epidemiological criteria* (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. *Please visit the WHO COVID-19 Case definition for details on clinical and epidemiological criteria. Updated 22 July 2023 Last 7 days ‘Last 7 days’ refers to the most recent complete epidemiological week (commonly referred to as an 'epi week'). Last 28 days ‘Last 28 days’ refers to the four preceding most recently complete epidemiological weeks. WHO Regions The World Health Organization (WHO) is divided into six regions with regional offices, each responsible for addressing health challenges and promoting public health within its designated geographical area. These regions serve as administrative units that allow the WHO to tailor its efforts to the specific needs, priorities, and health conditions of member countries within each region. World Bank Income Groups The World Bank classifies economies into income groups based on their Gross National Income (GNI) per capita. These annually updated classifications help the World Bank and other organizations analyze and understand global economic trends, allocate resources, and design development policies. Data sources COVID-19 case data From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data is compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported to WHO headquarters. WHO COVID-19 Dashboard is updated every Tuesday for the period of two full weeks prior. Counts primarily reflect laboratory-confirmed cases and deaths, based upon WHO case definitions; although some departures may exist due to local adaptations. Counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these data at a global level. All data represent date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data are subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals. New case and death counts from the Region of the Americas Starting from the week commencing on 11 September 2023, the source of the data from the Region of the Americas was switched to the aggregated national surveillances, received through the COVID-19, Influenza, RSV and Other Respiratory Viruses program in the Americas. Data have been included retrospectively since 31 July 2023. Rates <0.001 per 100,000 population may be rounded to 0. content: Skip to main content United Nations University Projects Commentary Science Talks Awards Careers Contact Toggle the UNU institute website header overlay About Our Work Our Team Learning Tools Publications News Events Search all content Search United Nations University Projects Experts Careers Our World 日本語 Toggle the UNU main website header overlay Institutes Topics Publications News Events Learning About Search all content Search About Our Work Our Team Learning Tools Publications News Events Projects Commentary Science Talks Awards Careers Contact UNU home United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health Toggle the menu overlay Search all content Search Open the keyword search overlay Close the keyword search overlay About Our Work Our Team Learning Tools Publications News Events Projects Commentary Science Talks Awards Careers Contact United Nations University Toggle the menu overlay Search all content Search Open the keyword search overlay Close the keyword search overlay Home UNU-INWEH News News Scientific Triumph, Equity Failure: Faster, Fairer COVID-19 Vaccine Roll-Out Could Have Saved Millions of Lives, UN University Publication Reveals Researchers call for an equity-focused global mechanism to improve vaccine financing, production and delivery before the next pandemic. Date Published 20 Oct 2026 Share Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Facebook Earlier and equitable access to COVID-19 vaccines could have saved millions of lives, particularly in lower-income countries. May 25, 2024/Shutterstock. Richmond Hill, Ontario, Canada (20 October 2026) – Beginning the global COVID-19 vaccine roll-out 100 days after the virus was sequenced could have saved more than 8 million lives by the end of 2021, most of them in lower-middle-income countries, according to modelling evidence brought together in a new Policy Brief from the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH). The authors argue that fair vaccine-sharing rules should be established before the next pandemic, rather than negotiated during the crisis itself. Best Practices in Global Vaccination Roll-Out to Reduce Health Inequity, written by researchers from UNU-INWEH, the University of Oxford, Imperial College London, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, King’s College London, Nagasaki University, Japan Institute for Health Security, Public Health Foundation of India, and the Middle East Liver Disease Center argues that international commitments to vaccine equity have not yet produced the operational mechanisms needed to deliver timely access across countries. It proposes an ‘equity-by-design’ framework that links vaccine development to financing, procurement, manufacturing, allocation, delivery, uptake, safety monitoring and accountability. It presents six recommendations as practical pillars for delivering on the WHO Pandemic Agreement, adopted in May 2025, and the amended International Health Regulations, in force for most States Parties since September 2025. The 8 million estimate comes from a modelling study reviewed in the publication, which assumes that the public health measures followed their historical course. An earlier start would have allowed high vaccine coverage to be reached before the Delta variant spread. The brief is equally clear that speed alone is not enough: parallel investment in vaccine manufacturing and health system infrastructure could have saved a further 3 million lives. The Policy Brief, accompanied by a peer-reviewed publication in the Expert Review of Vaccines journal in September 2026, highlights that COVID-19 vaccines were introduced across countries faster and more equitably than any earlier vaccine, whereas low-income countries often waited 10 to 30 years for vaccines against Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) and human papillomavirus (HPV). Even so, access remained sharply unequal. By the end of 2021, high- and upper-middle-income countries had administered at least one dose per person on average, compared with one for every three people in lower-middle-income countries and one for every 25 people in low-income countries. Studies reviewed in the publication estimate that if lower-middle- and low-income countries had matched the roll-out rates of high-income countries, as many as half of their COVID-19 deaths might have been averted by October 2021, and that sharing existing supply more equitably could have prevented 1.3 million deaths worldwide by the end of 2021. Delayed protection in lower-resource settings also prolonged transmission, raised the risk of new variants emerging and slowed economic recovery, weakening health and economic security across borders. “Effective pandemic preparedness requires clear allocation principles to be agreed before a crisis begins. When vaccine supplies are limited, distribution should respond to epidemiological evidence, including disease burden, risk of severe outcomes and the speed of transmission, so that vaccines reach the places where they can prevent the greatest harm,” said Dr. Mahan Ghafari, Wellcome Trust Early Career Research Fellow at the University of Oxford who led the investigation. “But for millions of people in poorer countries, they still arrived too late. The science moved at record speed while the systems for financing, sharing and delivering vaccines did not. Next time, the rules on who receives vaccines, and when, have to be agreed upon before the outbreak rather than negotiated in the middle of it.” The authors caution that regional manufacturing is not a stand-alone solution without long-term demand, predictable finance, regulatory convergence and a skilled workforce. They also argue that countries which report outbreaks and dangerous variants early should be supported rather than penalized, noting that punitive responses such as travel restrictions may have discouraged timely reporting during COVID-19. “COVID-19 proved wrong those who claimed that the virus would treat us all equally,” said Professor Kaveh Madani, Director of UNU-INWEH and a co-author of this publication. “Once again, we saw how a shared global threat can disproportionately harm the poor and less privileged. That experience taught us that we cannot rely on the speed of science and innovation alone. Before the next global emergency strikes, we must strengthen the foundations for equity through cooperative global mechanisms that can effectively improve financing, manufacturing and delivery, ensuring that life-saving solutions reach those who need them most.” The authors also call for sustained investment in pathogen genomic surveillance, including sequencing, analysis and workforce training across countries, to detect emerging threats and inform vaccine responses. Timely sharing of high-quality, geographically representative data should be encouraged through recognition of contributors and equitable access to benefits, including vaccines and other countermeasures, rather than punitive responses. Countries that detect and report a dangerous new variant early are doing the whole world a service, the research team believe. Vaccine equity requires more than statements of intent. This policy brief offers an equity-by-design framework that translates the principle into practical action across financing, procurement, allocation, surveillance, data sharing and delivery, so these mechanisms can be established before the next health emergency rather than improvised during it. Key Facts Starting the global vaccine roll-out 100 days after the virus was sequenced could have saved more than 8 million lives by the end of 2021, with the life-years saved valued at US$14 trillion. Parallel investment in manufacturing capacity and health systems could have saved a further 3 million lives and corresponded to a monetary saving of US$5 trillion. By the end of 2021, high- and upper-middle-income countries had administered at least one dose per person, against one dose for every 25 people in low-income countries. Had lower-middle- and low-income countries matched high-income roll-out rates, as many as half of their COVID-19 deaths might have been averted by 1 October 2021. Sharing existing vaccine supply more equitably could have prevented 1.3 million deaths worldwide by the end of 2021. Vaccination averted far fewer deaths per capita in low-income countries, particularly in the Eastern Mediterranean and African regions, than in high-income countries. Earlier vaccines, such as those against Hib and HPV, often reached low-income countries 10 to 30 years after high-income countries. Six steps to equity by design The brief sets out six policy recommendations for national governments, international organizations, vaccine manufacturers and the trusted voices who shape confidence in vaccination: Prepare before the next health emergency. Design pooled procurement mechanisms, fund research and development, and link pathogen surveillance to vaccine research, scalable manufacturing, supply chains and regional stockpiles before a crisis begins. Allocate vaccines equitably between nations. Build on the pooled demand and needs-based allocation of COVAX, adding earlier and predictable finance, enforceable access commitments, pre-defined dose-sharing triggers and public tracking of roll-out timelines. Secure timely and equitable vaccine procurement. Use advance purchase agreements that require transparent prices, flexible delivery and automatic dose-sharing under triggers agreed before an emergency, and diversify vaccine portfolios to reduce supply risks. Promote transparent data sharing and effective communication. Report cases, hospital admissions, deaths, vaccine adverse events and vaccination by age, sex, geography and risk group in standard, machine-readable formats, and plan community engagement and misinformation monitoring before a crisis. Insulate vaccine decisions from political distortion. Strengthen international regulatory standards, establish independent national advisory committees, and support rather than penalize countries that report outbreaks and variants early. Strengthen delivery systems and regional capacity. Invest in health facilities, trained health workers, cold chains and real-time stock and temperature monitoring, alongside regional manufacturing and products suited to low-resource and conflict-affected settings. Cross-cutting priority: within countries, target vaccines to vulnerable and high-risk groups using models that capture health and socio-economic vulnerability, with independent national oversight. Publication Information: Ghafari, M., Watson, O.J., Dascalu, S., Hsu Hnin Mon, S., Abeler-Dörner, L., Rezaee-Zavareh, M.S., Pley, C., Kordasti, S., Abbas, K., Panovska-Griffiths, J. and Madani, K. (2026). Best Practices in Global Vaccination Roll-Out to Reduce Health Inequity. United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH), Richmond Hill, Ontario, Canada. doi: 10.53328/INP26MAG001 Support Paper: Ghafari, M. et al. (2026). Global vaccine readiness: equity-by-design in pandemic preparedness and response. Expert Review of Vaccines. doi: 10.1080/14760584.2026.2732508 Available for Interview: Interview requests should be submitted to media.inweh@unu.edu About UNU-INWEH The United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH) is one of 13 institutions that make up the United Nations University (UNU), the academic arm of the United Nations. UNU-INWEH addresses critical water, environmental, and health challenges around the world. Through research, training, capacity development, and knowledge dissemination, the institute contributes to solving pressing global sustainability and human security issues of concern to the UN and its Member States. Headquartered in Richmond Hill, Ontario, UNU-INWEH has been hosted and supported by the Government of Canada since 1996 and has Hubs in Calgary, Hamburg, New York, Lund, and Pretoria. content: How Long Does COVID-19 Last? By Rachael Zimlich, BSN, RN Updated on October 23, 2026 Medically reviewed by Sanja Jelic, MD Add Us On Table of Contents View All Table of Contents Average Recovery Severe COVID Long COVID Factors Affecting Duration Shortenening Symptoms How Immunity Affects COVID Recovery Key Takeaways Mild to moderate COVID-19 symptoms usually last one to two weeks. Severe COVID-19 cases can take weeks or months to recover from. Long COVID symptoms can persist for months or even years. COVID-19 symptoms typically last one to two weeks, but the virus may stay in your body for longer. Some people may experience lingering effects, and various factors can influence recovery time. AnastasiaNurullina / Getty Images How Long Will Mild COVID-19 Symptoms Last? Mild to moderate COVID-19 infections typically last seven to 14 days, though some people recover in just a few days, while others may take longer. 1 Fatigue or a cough may last for a few weeks. Recovery varies by individual. Some people never develop symptoms, others experience mild to moderate illness, and some face life-threatening disease. Remember, your COVID infection can be contagious even without symptoms. You’re most contagious a day or two before symptoms start and during the first few days of illness. You can remain contagious for up to 10 days after symptoms begin. 2 How Long Does COVID Stay In Your System? The COVID-19 virus may stay in your body even after recovery. Studies have found the virus still present in stool (poop) for up to seven months in people with severe infections leading to long COVID. 3 A 2024 report found the virus present at 14 months, with some people having traces of COVID two years later despite not being sick. 4 What to Expect With Severe COVID-19 Severe or critical COVID-19 illness is most common in people over 50 and those with weakened immune systems or multiple health conditions. These infections often require hospitalization and can take several weeks or even months for recovery. Recovery time depends on how severe the COVID-19 infection is, whether complications such as pneumonia, blood clots, or organ damage occur, and if additional infections develop during treatment. 5 How Long Do Long COVID Symptoms Last? Long COVID , also called post-COVID syndrome, happens when symptoms last for three months or more after a COVID-19 infection. 6 About 10% of people with COVID infection will develop chronic symptoms, and even people with mild cases can develop long COVID. 7 Those facing greater risk include: 8 Women People whose infections were severe Those with underlying health conditions Unvaccinated people People may experience more than 200 different and evolving symptoms during COVID infection, and these can change, come and go, or continue after recovery. Symptoms have been reported anywhere from two weeks to months or even years. 9 Studies suggest that keeping your COVID vaccines up-to-date can reduce the risk of long COVID. Researchers continue to evaluate chronic COVID and the protective role of vaccination. 10 What Affects COVID-19 Duration? The specific variant that causes your COVID-19 infection has a lot to do with how long your illness lasts. However, additional factors can contribute to infection duration, such as: 11 Your age Having diabetes Having high blood pressure (hypertension) Whether you are immunocompromised Having obesity Being pregnant Talk with your healthcare provider about how cancer, kidney disease, and other conditions affect your COVID risk. 11 When to See Your Healthcare Provider You should let your healthcare provider know right away if your COVID test is positive, or you need testing. That’s all the more important if you’re over age 50 or have an underlying health issue that increases your risk of severe illness. Seek immediate care if you experience: 12 Trouble breathing Chest pain or pressure Confusion or trouble staying awake Pale, gray, or blue lips (cyanosis). A sign of low oxygen, it also can affect fingernails and skin. Can You Shorten How Long COVID Lasts? Maintaining good health habits can help strengthen your immune system to fight viruses like SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. You can also reduce your risk by practicing good hand hygiene and avoiding contact with people who are sick. Vaccination is another important tool. While vaccines don’t provide 100% protection, they can reduce both the severity and duration of COVID-19 if you become infected. 13 For people at higher risk of severe illness, prescription medications are available. When started within five to seven days of symptom onset, these treatments can help lower the risk of hospitalization or death from COVID-19. 14 The American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) recommends vaccination for adults 19 and older, especially those never vaccinated, people over 65, and those at higher risk of severe illness. 15 How Your Immunity Affects COVID-19 Recovery Even if you are vaccinated or have natural immunity from a previous infection, you can still catch COVID-19. The severity and length of illness depend on the strain that caused your current infection, the strain you were vaccinated against, and how long it’s been since your last infection or vaccination. Studies suggest that infections in vaccinated people can last as little as two days and are generally milder than infections in unvaccinated individuals. 13 Read More: Health A-Z Infectious Diseases Coronavirus (COVID-19) 15 Sources Verywell Health uses only high-quality sources, including peer-reviewed studies, to support the facts within our articles. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, October 20, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology Raman barcodes distinguish 20 SARS-CoV-2 variants in laboratory study by October 20, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Raman barcodes distinguish 20 SARS-CoV-2 variants in laboratory study Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A laboratory study led by Giuseppe Pezzotti at Kansai Medical University has shown that Raman spectroscopy can distinguish 20 SARS-CoV-2 strains and subvariants by detecting structural characteristics of their RNA rather than directly determining the viruses’ complete nucleotide sequences. The researchers converted characteristic patterns of molecular vibrations into what they call “Raman barcodes,” which separated every strain and subvariant in the tested collection. The experimental findings were published online in Advanced Science on September 30, 2026, and establish an initial foundation for a proposed “Raman genome” approach to molecular identification. The study addresses the fact that viral RNA contains information beyond the order and abundance of its four nucleotide bases. RNA molecules fold into complex three-dimensional structures through interactions between neighboring nucleotides and complementary bases. These secondary structures can include hairpins, stems and paired regions, and they can differ among viruses even when their overall nucleotide composition appears remarkably similar. Raman spectroscopy detects characteristic molecular vibrations when a sample interacts with light. In the experiment, the resulting signals reflected contributions from the RNA backbone, ribose rings, phosphate linkages and nitrogenous bases, allowing the investigators to characterize patterns associated with RNA organization rather than reading the sequence letter by letter. Discover more Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges For the experiment, the team extracted RNA nucleotide strands from 20 SARS-CoV-2 strains. The panel comprised the original Japanese isolate, seven named non-Omicron variants—Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Theta and Mu—and 12 Omicron subvariants. The researchers systematically acquired the Raman spectra of these samples and mathematically deconvoluted them to identify their individual molecular components. All samples shared characteristic signals associated with common RNA chemistry, including the backbone, ribofuranose rings, phosphate groups and nitrogenous bases. At the same time, subtle but reproducible differences emerged among the strains and subvariants. Discover more Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Read Med Journals Compare Lab Gear Those differences were then encoded as Raman barcodes, defined in the study as characteristic patterns of Raman signals that capture distinctive molecular features of viral RNA. The approach was intended to preserve structural information that might not be apparent from a simple comparison of nucleotide composition. In the authors’ conception, a “Raman genome” represents an RNA genome through its molecular architecture and spectral fingerprint rather than through a direct reading of its nucleotide sequence. This is a conceptual extension of genome characterization: the barcode captures molecular features associated with RNA folding and conformation, including the physical contributions of the sugar-phosphate framework, ribose and the bases. A central finding was that the observed spectral distinctions could not be explained only by variation in the relative abundance of the four RNA bases. When the genome sequences were used to assess those proportions, the investigated strains had highly similar base fractions. Their Raman spectra nevertheless exhibited markedly different molecular signatures. This separation between sequence-based composition and measured spectra indicates that the Raman measurement was sensitive to information beyond base abundance. The authors investigated the molecular origins of the differences by relating particular Raman bands to features of RNA secondary structure, including backbone conformation, nucleotide-chain characteristics, ribofuranose dynamics, hairpin formation, stem length and base-pairing environments. The resulting barcodes discriminated all 20 strains and subvariants examined, including multiple Omicron subvariants. Conventional principal component analysis, by comparison, provided only limited separation among the same material. The distinction between these two analyses is important to the reported result: the successful classification was based on explicitly encoded Raman spectral features, rather than on the limited discrimination produced by the conventional PCA approach. The finding also shows why the spectral differences matter. They were not merely an incidental effect of broad base composition; instead, selected bands could be associated with interpretable structural features of the RNA strands and used to distinguish the tested panel. Technical interpretation of the spectra depends partly on changes in Raman signal intensity caused by molecular interactions. Hyperchromic and hypochromic responses involving nitrogenous bases provide clues about pairing environments and RNA secondary structure. Bands associated with ribose vibrations, phosphate linkages and RNA backbone conformation also contribute to the encoded barcode. These physically interpretable features connect the classification result to molecular architecture rather than leaving it as an unexplained statistical separation. The work therefore combines two aspects of the proposed method: a Raman fingerprint capable of differentiating samples and an analysis linking parts of that fingerprint to secondary-structure characteristics such as stem formation, hairpins and the environments in which bases are paired. Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms Order DNA Kits Get a POS System Biology textbook sales The researchers present the result as a first step toward a broader strategy for characterizing viral RNA through spectroscopy. They propose that future development could combine physically interpretable Raman markers with automated spectral analysis, theoretical calculations and artificial intelligence. Such systems could potentially provide a rapid layer of molecular information alongside sequencing, particularly during outbreaks, epidemics and emergency or critical-care situations where timely characterization may be important. The release does not report the implementation of such a clinical system. The reported evidence concerns an experimental comparison of RNA strands from a defined set of 20 strains and subvariants, not prospective surveillance or routine diagnostic validation. Several limitations follow directly from that experimental scope. The panel was limited to 20 SARS-CoV-2 strains and subvariants, so the result demonstrates discrimination within the tested collection rather than universal performance across the full diversity of SARS-CoV-2 or other viruses. The researchers used RNA nucleotide strands extracted from the strains, meaning the measurements were performed downstream of sample preparation and did not by themselves demonstrate direct identification in unprocessed patient material. The news release also does not report prospective clinical comparisons, blinded diagnostic performance, turnaround time, cost, sensitivity, specificity or reproducibility across laboratories. It likewise does not describe testing under changing sample conditions or a clinical workflow for detecting newly emerging variants. Even with these qualifications, the experiments offer a technically distinct route for viral science. Conventional sequencing determines the order of nucleotides, whereas the proposed Raman method captures a molecular fingerprint associated with RNA structure and conformation. By successfully discriminating 20 strains and subvariants whose evaluated base fractions were highly similar, the study shows that structural variation supplied information that was not captured by simple composition estimates alone. The authors do not claim that Raman analysis will replace RNA sequencing. Instead, they describe it as a complementary approach that may eventually support faster variant screening and broaden molecular surveillance. The work was financially supported by a Japan Society for the Promotion of Science grant, and the authors declared no conflicts of interest. content: A pooled analysis from the global SCORPIO clinical program showed potent antiviral activity with ensitrelvir across age, vaccination status and risk for severe disease New data underscores that even mild-to-moderate COVID-19 may worsen and exacerbate underlying chronic conditions, supporting the importance of prevention OSAKA, Japan--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Shionogi & Co., Ltd. (Head Office: Osaka, Japan; Chief Executive Officer: Isao Teshirogi, Ph.D.; hereafter “Shionogi”) will present new exploratory analyses from the global Phase 3 SCORPIO-PEP study, virology data from across the ensitrelvir phase 3 program, and new insights on the continued burden of COVID-19 at IDWeek 2026. XOCOVA ® (ensitrelvir) was approved in May 2026 by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) of COVID‐19 in adults and adolescents 12 years of age and older following contact with an individual who has COVID-19. 1 The approval was based on positive results from SCORPIO-PEP, a global, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study. In the primary analysis population, XOCOVA significantly reduced the risk of developing symptomatic COVID-19 by 67% in individuals following exposure to an infected individual through Day 10 compared with placebo (ensitrelvir n=1,030; placebo n=1,011). 1,2 In SCORPIO-PEP, XOCOVA was generally well tolerated, with similar rates of adverse events across groups (15.1% in the ensitrelvir group (n=1,190) and 15.5% in the placebo group (n=1,187)). 2 The most common adverse events (regardless of causality) occurring in greater than or equal to 1% of the XOCOVA group and at a greater frequency compared to placebo were headache, diarrhea, and cough. 1,2 There were no reports of altered taste (dysgeusia) attributed to XOCOVA in the trial. 2,3 Exploratory SCORPIO-PEP Analyses Describe Symptom Severity and Viral Outcomes Among Participants with Breakthrough Infection or Infection Present at Baseline In an oral presentation at IDWeek 2026, Shionogi will report new exploratory analyses from the SCORPIO-PEP study evaluating participants who had breakthrough infections or were already infected at baseline. 4 Among breakthrough infection cases (based on RT-PCR positivity regardless of symptoms) in the primary analysis population, the mean maximum viral RNA levels were lower in participants receiving ensitrelvir compared to those receiving placebo (3.1 vs 4.3 mean log10 copies/mL, respectively, seen in 144 and 217 breakthrough infection cases, respectively). 4 In household contacts who were infected with SARS-CoV-2 at the time of enrollment (confirmed positive by baseline central RT-PCR despite testing negative on a local screening test and being asymptomatic; n=237), numerically lower mean viral RNA levels were also observed with ensitrelvir in comparison to placebo on Days 3 and 6. 4 In the primary analysis population, a numerically lower proportion of participants with symptomatic breakthrough infections taking ensitrelvir developed severe symptoms, compared with those taking placebo (severe symptoms were reported in 8/28 or 28.6% of individuals receiving ensitrelvir compared with 48/89 or 53.9% of individuals receiving placebo). 4 Similarly, numerically lower mean total symptom scores earlier in the study and lower mean maximum total symptom scores were observed in participants receiving ensitrelvir compared with placebo (mean maximum total scores were 6.6 vs 8.9 respectively). 4 In participants receiving ensitrelvir who were infected with SARS-CoV-2 at the time of enrollment despite testing negative on a local screening test and being asymptomatic, a numerically lower proportion developed severe symptoms compared with placebo (severe symptoms were reported in 2/18 or 11.1% of individuals receiving ensitrelvir compared with 9/24 or 37.5% of individuals receiving placebo). 4 Similarly, numerically lower mean total symptom scores earlier in the study and mean maximum total symptom scores were observed in those receiving ensitrelvir compared with placebo. 4 “SCORPIO-PEP showed that early administration of ensitrelvir following household exposure reduced the risk of symptomatic COVID-19,” said Simon Portsmouth, MD, FRCP, Senior Vice President, Head of Clinical Development, Shionogi Inc. “This exploratory analysis provides additional insight into the antiviral activity of ensitrelvir on viral load and symptom outcomes among participants who developed COVID-19. These observations add to our understanding of the potential outcomes associated with early administration of ensitrelvir following household exposure.” Pooled Phase 3 Study Data Analysis Shows Potent Antiviral Activity of Ensitrelvir Through Observed Reductions in Infectious Virus In a separate poster presentation, investigators will report findings from a post-hoc pooled analysis of two Phase 3 studies designed to assess infectious-virus-based virologic outcomes across a broad range of participants with confirmed COVID-19 infection. 6 Unlike viral RNA detection by RT-PCR, which may identify noninfectious viral remnants, infectious-virus measurements assess the presence of replication-competent virus and can provide additional insight into antiviral activity. 5,6 By Day 4, participants who received ensitrelvir (375 mg on Day 1, then 125 mg on Days 2–5; n=484) had numerically greater reductions in infectious virus titers than those who received placebo (n=487) (difference in least-squares mean of 0.21 log10 TCID 50 /mL). 6 Similar results were observed across subgroups regardless of age, vaccination status, and risk factors for severe COVID-19. Also on day 4, a higher proportion of ensitrelvir recipients had undetectable infectious viral load compared to those receiving placebo (95.7% [463/484] vs 72.1% [351/487]). 6 “With data pooled from two Phase 3 studies, this analysis represents the most extensive infectious virus dataset reported for a COVID-19 antiviral to date, and it helps to further characterize ensitrelvir’s effect on active viral replication,” said Florin Draica, MD, CMD, MBA, Senior Vice President, U.S. Medical Affairs, Shionogi Inc. “Although these results are exploratory, the observed reductions in infectious virus provide additional support of ensitrelvir’s antiviral activity and warrant further evaluation of their potential implications for infectivity and transmission.” Systematic Literature Review Highlights the Continued Burden of COVID-19 and Its Impact on Underlying Chronic Conditions Shionogi will also present a systematic literature review evaluating the impact of acute COVID-19 on individuals with underlying chronic conditions during the Omicron era or in earlier time periods. The review included 35 observational studies assessing clinical outcomes, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and healthcare resource utilization (HCRU). 7 Across the studies reviewed, acute COVID-19 was associated with worsening, exacerbation, or relapse of underlying chronic conditions spanning respiratory, neurologic, cardiovascular, renal, and other disease areas. 7 More than half of studies evaluating clinical outcomes (17 out of 33) reported statistically significant worsening of underlying chronic conditions such as asthma, COPD, multiple sclerosis and CKD, following acute COVID-19. 7 COVID-19 was also associated with worsening outcomes in five of eight studies reporting on HRQoL and increased hospitalization frequency or extended hospital length of stay in four of the six studies reporting on HCRU. 7 “Across studies in this review, acute COVID-19 during the Omicron predominance was associated with worsening or exacerbation of underlying chronic conditions. Specifically, we found that COVID-19 infection, even mild or moderate, was associated with reduced health-related quality of life and increased healthcare resource utilization,” said Alpesh N. Amin, M.D., Professor, Founding Chief and Executive Director of Hospital Medicine & Palliative Medicine, and Co-Director & Medical Director of the Institute for Precision Health at the University of California, Irvine. “These findings reinforce the continued burden of COVID-19 and underscore the importance of prevention, especially among people living with chronic conditions.” The Ongoing Impact of COVID-19 COVID-19 remains highly transmissible, driven by Omicron and its subvariants, and up to 47% of people living with an infected individual may develop COVID-19. 8,9 The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that between October 1, 2025, and September 26, 2026, there were 5.2-14.6 million new cases in the U.S., resulting in 1.1-2.7 million outpatient visits, 170,000-270,000 hospitalizations and 17,000-48,000 deaths. 10 Beyond acute infection, COVID-19, even mild-to-moderate, may worsen underlying chronic conditions and can have lasting health impacts. Studies have reported increased rates of new and worsening neurologic, cardiovascular, respiratory, and chronic kidney conditions in the year following COVID-19 infection. 11-19 COVID-19 also disproportionately affects older adults with greater risk for severe illness and death in close-community settings, such as long-term care facilities. 20 About SCORPIO-PEP The global, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study, SCORPIO-PEP, assessed the safety and efficacy of XOCOVA as post-exposure prophylaxis for COVID-19. The study was conducted from June 2023-September 2024. It included 2,387 study participants aged 12 years and older with a negative local screening test for SARS-CoV-2 infection and no symptoms at the time of enrollment, who were exposed to a person living in their household with symptomatic COVID-19. More than 98% of household contacts tested positive for antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 N (nucleocapsid) or S (spike) proteins, indicating that nearly all had evidence of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection or vaccination, or both. Study participants were randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to receive XOCOVA (375 mg on Day 1 and 125 mg on Days 2-5) or placebo, once daily for five days, and began treatment within 72 hours of when the household member with COVID-19 began showing symptoms. Results from SCORPIO-PEP were published in the New England Journal of Medicine . SCORPIO-PEP is the first and only Phase 3 study of an oral antiviral to meet the primary endpoint of preventing COVID-19 following exposure to an infected individual.* About XOCOVA XOCOVA ® (ensitrelvir) is a SARS-CoV-2 main protease inhibitor created through joint research between Hokkaido University and Shionogi. SARS-CoV-2 has an enzyme called the main protease, which is essential for the replication of the virus. XOCOVA suppresses the replication of SARS-CoV-2 by selectively inhibiting the main protease. XOCOVA is approved in the U.S., Japan and European Union for post-exposure prophylaxis of COVID‐19 in adults and adolescents 12 years of age and older following contact with an individual who has COVID-19. XOCOVA received emergency regulatory approval in Japan in November 2022 and full approval in March 2024 for the treatment of COVID-19 in adults and adolescents 12 years of age and older. XOCOVA received supplemental approval in Japan in June 2026 for pediatric patients aged 6 to under 12 years who weigh at least 20 kg for the treatment of COVID-19. XOCOVA is not approved for the treatment of COVID-19 in the U.S. U.S. INDICATION XOCOVA (ensitrelvir) is a prescription medicine used to help prevent coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in adults and children aged 12 years and older following contact with a person who has COVID-19 (post-exposure prophylaxis). It is not known if XOCOVA is safe and effective in children under age 12. IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION Do not take XOCOVA if you are: allergic to ensitrelvir or any of the ingredients in XOCOVA. take any of the following medicines, as these may interact with XOCOVA and may cause severe or life-threatening side effects or death: apalutamide, carbamazepine, colchicine, dihydroergotamine, enzalutamide, eplerenone, ergotamine, finerenone, ivabradine, lomitapide, lumacaftor/ivacaftor, lurasidone, methylergonovine, phenytoin, pimozide, quinidine, rifampin, St. John’s wort, simvastatin, triazolam or voclosporin. These are not the only medicines that may cause serious or life-threatening side effects if taken with XOCOVA. XOCOVA may increase or decrease the levels of many medicines in your body. Tell your healthcare provider (HCP) about all the medicines you take because additional laboratory tests or dose changes of your other medicines may be necessary during XOCOVA use. Your HCP may tell you about specific symptoms to watch for that may indicate you need to stop or decrease the dose of some of your other medicines. Before taking XOCOVA, tell your HCP about all your medical conditions, including if you: are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. XOCOVA may harm your unborn baby. For females who are able to become pregnant, your HCP will check with you to see if you are pregnant before starting XOCOVA. Use effective birth control (contraception) during XOCOVA use and for 2 weeks after the final dose. Tell your HCP right away if you become pregnant or think you may be pregnant during XOCOVA use. are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. It is not known if XOCOVA passes into your breast milk. Do not breastfeed during XOCOVA use and for 2 weeks after the final dose. Tell your HCP about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements. Your HCP can tell you if it is safe to take XOCOVA with other medicines. Do not start a new medicine without telling your HCP. What are the possible side effects of XOCOVA? XOCOVA may cause serious side effects, including: Allergic reactions, including severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis). Stop taking XOCOVA and get medical help right away if you get any of the following allergic reaction symptoms: skin rash; hives; itching; swelling of the mouth, lips, tongue, or face; trouble swallowing or breathing; throat tightness; dizziness or feeling lightheaded; stomach-area (abdomen) pain; or vomiting. The most common side effects of XOCOVA include : headache, diarrhea, and cough. These are not all possible side effects of XOCOVA. For more info, ask your HCP or pharmacist. You are encouraged to report negative side effects of prescription drugs to the FDA. Visit www.fda.gov/medwatch or call 1-800-FDA-1088 . Please see full Prescribing Information , including Patient Information , for XOCOVA. About Shionogi Inc. Shionogi Inc. is a U.S. subsidiary of Shionogi & Co., Ltd., a global research‐driven pharmaceutical company. Since 1878, Shionogi has been developing new treatments to improve patients’ lives worldwide. Today in North America, we are focused on infectious and rare diseases, and our portfolio includes an antibiotic for serious infections caused by susceptible Gram-negative bacteria, an oral antiviral for post-exposure prophylaxis of COVID-19 and a therapy for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Together with our subsidiaries Qpex Biopharma Inc. and Shionogi Canada Inc., we are continuing to innovate across infectious disease, rare disease and additional high‐need therapeutic areas. Learn more at shionogi.com . About Shionogi & Co., Ltd. Shionogi & Co., Ltd. is a 148-year-old global, research-driven pharmaceutical company headquartered in Osaka, Japan, that is dedicated to bringing benefits to patients based on its corporate philosophy of “supplying the best possible medicine to protect the health and wellbeing of the patients we serve.” The company currently markets products in several therapeutic areas including anti-infectives, pain and CNS disorders. Shionogi’s research and development currently targets two therapeutic areas: infectious diseases and diseases with unmet medical needs, including rare diseases, allergy/inflammation, oncology, hearing loss, and sleep apnea. For more information on Shionogi & Co., Ltd., please visit https://www.shionogi.com/global/en . Forward-Looking Statements This announcement contains forward-looking statements. Risks and uncertainties include general domestic and international economic conditions such as general industry and market conditions, and changes of interest rate and currency exchange rate. Also for existing products, there are manufacturing and marketing risks, which include, but are not limited to, inability to build production capacity to meet demand, lack of availability of raw materials and entry of competitive products. content: Advanced Search Home News Releases Multimedia Meetings Login Register News Release 20-Oct-2026 “Raman Genome” for SARS-CoV-2: new Raman technology distinguishes viral variants by their molecular RNA architecture Identifying 20 SARS-CoV-2 variants and subvariants without RNA sequencing Peer-Reviewed Publication Kansai Medical University Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: Raman spectroscopy can quantitatively unfold the secondary RNA structures of SARS-CoV-2 variants/subvariants, allowing their spectroscopic identification and consequent Raman barcode classification. This finding opens the way to a new “Raman genome” approach of general validity in virology. The image was not created using AI. The author created the image using PowerPoint. view more Credit: Distinguished Professor Giuseppe Pezzotti from Kansai Medical University, Japan. A research team led by Distinguished Professor Giuseppe Pezzotti at the Biomedical Engineering Center, Kansai Medical University (Chairman: Toshio Yamashita; President: Tatsuo Kinashi; Japan), has demonstrated that differences in the molecular structures of viral RNA can be captured as “Raman barcodes,” enabling the identification of 20 SARS-CoV-2 variants and subvariants. These findings are expected to contribute to the development of a rapid method for identifying newly emerging viral variants. The findings were published online in Advanced Science journal on September 30, 2026. Background of the Research The identification and surveillance of viral variants have traditionally relied on RNA sequencing, which provides detailed information about the nucleotide sequence of a virus but requires long procedures using specialized instrumentation, sample processing, and computational analysis. However, viral RNA is more than a simple sequence of the four genetic bases. RNA molecules fold into complex three-dimensional structures through interactions between neighboring nucleotides and complementary bases. These secondary structures can influence how RNA behaves biologically and can differ even when the overall nucleotide composition appears remarkably similar. Raman spectroscopy is capable of instantaneously reading such structures. The researchers therefore asked a fundamental question: Can the molecular vibrations of viral RNA provide a distinctive fingerprint of different viral variants, even when their conventional genetic composition appears highly similar? Raman spectroscopy offers a direct way to probe molecular vibrations. Instead of reading the RNA sequence letter by letter, it captures a molecular vibrational fingerprint arising from the RNA backbone, ribose rings, phosphate linkages, and nitrogenous bases. The study introduces the concept of encoding these fingerprints as Raman barcodes, providing the basis for a new concept of a “Raman genome.” Overview of the Research RNA nucleotide strands were extracted from 20 SARS-CoV-2 strains, comprising the original Japanese isolate, Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Theta, Mu, and 12 Omicron subvariants. The Raman spectra of these RNAs were systematically acquired and mathematically deconvoluted to identify their individual molecular components. Although all samples shared characteristic signals associated with the RNA backbone, ribofuranose rings, phosphate groups, and nitrogenous bases, subtle but reproducible differences emerged among the strains. Importantly, these differences were not simply a reflection of differences in the relative abundance of the four RNA bases. The investigated strains showed highly similar base fractions when evaluated from their genome sequences, yet their Raman spectra exhibited markedly different molecular signatures. The researchers therefore encoded the characteristic spectral features into Raman barcodes. Unlike conventional principal component analysis, which provided only limited separation, the Raman barcode approach successfully differentiated all 20 investigated strains and subvariants. The molecular origins of these differences were further explored by relating specific Raman bands to features of RNA secondary structure, including backbone conformation, nucleotide chain characteristics, ribofuranose dynamics, hairpin formation, stem length, and base-pairing environments. Research Outcomes The study represents a first step toward defining a “Raman genome”: a spectroscopic fingerprint capable of characterizing viral RNA according to its molecular architecture rather than solely according to its nucleotide sequence. The major scientific advances are: 1. Molecular discrimination beyond conventional genetic composition The study demonstrates that SARS-CoV-2 RNAs with remarkably similar nucleotide compositions can nevertheless exhibit substantially different Raman fingerprints. This indicates that Raman spectroscopy is sensitive to structural information encoded in RNA beyond simple base abundance. 2. Successful discrimination of 20 SARS-CoV-2 variants and subvariants Raman barcodes provided clear discrimination among all 20 investigated strains, including multiple Omicron subvariants, whereas conventional principal component analysis (PCA) showed limited discriminatory capability. 3. Linking Raman signals to RNA secondary structure Rather than treating the Raman spectrum as a purely statistical fingerprint, the study identifies physically interpretable molecular markers associated with ribose vibrations, phosphate linkages, RNA backbone conformation, and hyperchromic or hypochromic responses of nitrogenous bases affected by pairing and secondary structure environments. 4. A potential new tool for rapid variant screening Because the approach is based on Raman analysis of extracted RNA rather than complete RNA sequencing, it could ultimately provide a rapid screening strategy for emerging viral variants. Such an approach would be particularly valuable in emergency and critical-care situations, where obtaining molecular information rapidly can be crucial. 5. Toward a new generation of molecular diagnostics The concept extends Raman spectroscopy from conventional chemical identification toward molecular-scale diagnostics of biological information. Future developments may combine physically interpretable Raman markers with automated spectral analysis, theoretical calculations, and artificial intelligence to create increasingly powerful predictive systems. Significance to society The findings could contribute to the development of faster and more accessible approaches for viral surveillance and molecular diagnostics. Because Raman analysis can potentially characterize viral RNA without performing complete RNA sequencing, it may ultimately enable rapid screening of emerging variants when timely information is particularly important, such as during outbreaks, epidemics, and emergency or critical-care situations. More broadly, the “Raman genome” concept could open a new field in molecular medicine and microbiology in which the structural state of nucleic acids is investigated directly through their molecular fingerprints. With further technological development, automation, and integration with artificial intelligence, Raman-based molecular fingerprints could complement conventional sequencing and provide an additional, rapid layer of information for identifying and monitoring emerging pathogens. Glossary 1. Raman barcode A characteristic pattern of Raman signals obtained from a biological molecule or sample. In this study, Raman barcodes encode the distinctive molecular features of viral RNA and allow different SARS-CoV-2 strains to be distinguished. 2. RNA sequencing A technology that determines the nucleotide sequence of RNA. It is currently an important method for identifying and characterizing viral variants. The Raman approach investigated in this study is intended as a complementary, rather than replacement, technology. 3. Raman spectroscopy A technique that identifies molecules by analyzing the characteristic vibrations they produce when interacting with light. It provides a molecular “fingerprint” of a sample without requiring it to be chemically labeled. 4. RNA backbone The repeating structural framework of an RNA molecule, composed primarily of ribose sugars and phosphate groups. Raman signals from the backbone provide information about the conformation and organization of the RNA chain. 5.“Raman genome” A new concept proposed in this study in which the molecular architecture of an RNA genome is represented by its Raman spectral fingerprint. Unlike conventional genome sequencing, it does not read the nucleotide sequence directly but captures molecular information associated with RNA structure and conformation. 6. RNA secondary structure The three-dimensional folding patterns formed within an RNA molecule through interactions between its nucleotides. These structures include features such as stems, loops, and hairpins and can influence the physical and biological properties of RNA. 7. Hyperchromic/hypochromic effect Changes in the intensity of Raman signals caused by molecular interactions, particularly changes in the environment and pairing of RNA bases. In this study, such intensity changes provide clues about RNA secondary structure. *** Reference DOI: 10.1002/advs.77679 Funding information This work was financially supported by Japan Society for the Promotion of Science [Grant Number JP23K09359]. title: Raman barcodes distinguish 20 SARS-CoV-2 variants in laboratory study
excerpt: A laboratory study used Raman barcodes to distinguish 20 SARS-CoV-2 strains and subvariants through RNA molecular architecture rather than nucleotide sequencing alone.

content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, October 20, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology Raman barcodes distinguish 20 SARS-CoV-2 variants in laboratory study by October 20, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Raman barcodes distinguish 20 SARS-CoV-2 variants in laboratory study Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A laboratory study led by Giuseppe Pezzotti at Kansai Medical University has shown that Raman spectroscopy can distinguish 20 SARS-CoV-2 strains and subvariants by detecting structural characteristics of their RNA rather than directly determining the viruses’ complete nucleotide sequences. The researchers converted characteristic patterns of molecular vibrations into what they call “Raman barcodes,” which separated every strain and subvariant in the tested collection. The experimental findings were published online in Advanced Science on September 30, 2026, and establish an initial foundation for a proposed “Raman genome” approach to molecular identification. The study addresses the fact that viral RNA contains information beyond the order and abundance of its four nucleotide bases. RNA molecules fold into complex three-dimensional structures through interactions between neighboring nucleotides and complementary bases. These secondary structures can include hairpins, stems and paired regions, and they can differ among viruses even when their overall nucleotide composition appears remarkably similar. Raman spectroscopy detects characteristic molecular vibrations when a sample interacts with light. In the experiment, the resulting signals reflected contributions from the RNA backbone, ribose rings, phosphate linkages and nitrogenous bases, allowing the investigators to characterize patterns associated with RNA organization rather than reading the sequence letter by letter. For the experiment, the team extracted RNA nucleotide strands from 20 SARS-CoV-2 strains. The panel comprised the original Japanese isolate, seven named non-Omicron variants—Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, Theta and Mu—and 12 Omicron subvariants. The researchers systematically acquired the Raman spectra of these samples and mathematically deconvoluted them to identify their individual molecular components. All samples shared characteristic signals associated with common RNA chemistry, including the backbone, ribofuranose rings, phosphate groups and nitrogenous bases. At the same time, subtle but reproducible differences emerged among the strains and subvariants. Those differences were then encoded as Raman barcodes, defined in the study as characteristic patterns of Raman signals that capture distinctive molecular features of viral RNA. The approach was intended to preserve structural information that might not be apparent from a simple comparison of nucleotide composition. In the authors’ conception, a “Raman genome” represents an RNA genome through its molecular architecture and spectral fingerprint rather than through a direct reading of its nucleotide sequence. This is a conceptual extension of genome characterization: the barcode captures molecular features associated with RNA folding and conformation, including the physical contributions of the sugar-phosphate framework, ribose and the bases. A central finding was that the observed spectral distinctions could not be explained only by variation in the relative abundance of the four RNA bases. When the genome sequences were used to assess those proportions, the investigated strains had highly similar base fractions. Their Raman spectra nevertheless exhibited markedly different molecular signatures. This separation between sequence-based composition and measured spectra indicates that the Raman measurement was sensitive to information beyond base abundance. The authors investigated the molecular origins of the differences by relating particular Raman bands to features of RNA secondary structure, including backbone conformation, nucleotide-chain characteristics, ribofuranose dynamics, hairpin formation, stem length and base-pairing environments. The resulting barcodes discriminated all 20 strains and subvariants examined, including multiple Omicron subvariants. Conventional principal component analysis, by comparison, provided only limited separation among the same material. The distinction between these two analyses is important to the reported result: the successful classification was based on explicitly encoded Raman spectral features, rather than on the limited discrimination produced by the conventional PCA approach. The finding also shows why the spectral differences matter. They were not merely an incidental effect of broad base composition; instead, selected bands could be associated with interpretable structural features of the RNA strands and used to distinguish the tested panel. Technical interpretation of the spectra depends partly on changes in Raman signal intensity caused by molecular interactions. Hyperchromic and hypochromic responses involving nitrogenous bases provide clues about pairing environments and RNA secondary structure. Bands associated with ribose vibrations, phosphate linkages and RNA backbone conformation also contribute to the encoded barcode. These physically interpretable features connect the classification result to molecular architecture rather than leaving it as an unexplained statistical separation. The work therefore combines two aspects of the proposed method: a Raman fingerprint capable of differentiating samples and an analysis linking parts of that fingerprint to secondary-structure characteristics such as stem formation, hairpins and the environments in which bases are paired. The researchers present the result as a first step toward a broader strategy for characterizing viral RNA through spectroscopy. They propose that future development could combine physically interpretable Raman markers with automated spectral analysis, theoretical calculations and artificial intelligence. Such systems could potentially provide a rapid layer of molecular information alongside sequencing, particularly during outbreaks, epidemics and emergency or critical-care situations where timely characterization may be important. The release does not report the implementation of such a clinical system. The reported evidence concerns an experimental comparison of RNA strands from a defined set of 20 strains and subvariants, not prospective surveillance or routine diagnostic validation. Several limitations follow directly from that experimental scope. The panel was limited to 20 SARS-CoV-2 strains and subvariants, so the result demonstrates discrimination within the tested collection rather than universal performance across the full diversity of SARS-CoV-2 or other viruses. The researchers used RNA nucleotide strands extracted from the strains, meaning the measurements were performed downstream of sample preparation and did not by themselves demonstrate direct identification in unprocessed patient material. The news release also does not report prospective clinical comparisons, blinded diagnostic performance, turnaround time, cost, sensitivity, specificity or reproducibility across laboratories. It likewise does not describe testing under changing sample conditions or a clinical workflow for detecting newly emerging variants. Even with these qualifications, the experiments offer a technically distinct route for viral science. Conventional sequencing determines the order of nucleotides, whereas the proposed Raman method captures a molecular fingerprint associated with RNA structure and conformation. By successfully discriminating 20 strains and subvariants whose evaluated base fractions were highly similar, the study shows that structural variation supplied information that was not captured by simple composition estimates alone. The authors do not claim that Raman analysis will replace RNA sequencing. Instead, they describe it as a complementary approach that may eventually support faster variant screening and broaden molecular surveillance. The work was financially supported by a Japan Society for the Promotion of Science grant, and the authors declared no conflicts of interest.
