The committee will examine evidence involving children, adolescents, working-age adults, and older adults and consider implications for military force readiness, military and veteran health, and health system planning. The committee will examine eight questions: 1. What is the current state of scientific evidence regarding the direct effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection on neurocognitive function across the lifespan, including children, adolescents, working-age adults, and older adults? 2. Which cognitive domains are most consistently affected following SARS-CoV-2 infection, based on validated neuropsychological, educational, occupational, and functional metrics? 3. What evidence exists from laboratory, clinical, neuroimaging, neuropathological, and mechanistic studies regarding the biological pathways by which SARS-CoV-2 may affect neuronal function, neuroinflammation, cerebrovascular integrity, synaptic processes, or neurodevelopment? 4. How do neurocognitive outcomes differ based on the severity of initial infection, reinfection, and the presence or absence of post-acute sequelae? 5. What is known about the impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection on children and adolescents, including effects on: Learning, academic performance, and school-based cognitive metrics Attention, executive function, memory, and developmental milestones Attendance, special education needs, and standardized testing outcomes, where studied Potential impact of these effects on military recruitment, service, and performance 6. What evidence exists regarding neurocognitive impacts in adults, including effects on: Occupational performance and functional capacity Complex cognitive tasks relevant to military and civilian work settings Aging trajectories and interactions with underlying medical conditions 7. What is the strength of evidence for the protective effects of COVID-19 vaccination against: Neurocognitive impairment following infection Long COVID-associated cognitive symptoms Repeated infections and cumulative cognitive risk 8. What gaps remain in the evidence base, and what research approaches would most effectively address unanswered questions of relevance to military and veteran populations? The committee will also consider implications for: Force readiness, training, performance, and retention Long-term health trajectories of service members Aging and medically complex veteran populations Occupational and cognitive demands specific to military service Health system planning within military and veteran contexts The committee will develop a report containing findings and conclusions on the questions above. It will not make recommendations. Dr. Becker’s research focuses on the impact of infectious diseases on neurocognition. She has gained an international reputation for her work on the cognitive effects of long COVID and other infection-associated chronic conditions. She is a multiple Principal Investigator on a National Institutes of Health (NIH) study examining plasma tau biomarkers of post-COVID-19 cognitive impairment and Principal Investigator of an NIH/National Institute of Mental Health clinical trial treating cognitive impairment and depression in long COVID. She is Neurocognitive Lead for the NIH RECOVER 2.0 and RECOVER-TLC trials and was multiple Principal Investigator of NIH’s RECOVER-Neuro trial. She is also co-investigator of related grants, including an Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality grant establishing an integrated long COVID and primary care clinic and an NIH/National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) study investigating mechanisms of neurological sequelae of COVID-19. She chairs the NIH/NINDS Cognitive Assessments Common Data Elements ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome) Committee and the International Neuropsychological Society’s NeuroCOVID Committee and serves as an expert panelist on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Council of Medical Specialty Societies Long COVID Education and Care Management panel. Dr. Becker completed her doctoral training at Fordham, residency at Harvard Medical School/Massachusetts General Hospital, and neuropsychology fellowship at Northwell Health. She previously served on the National Academies’ Committee on the Long-Term Health Effects Stemming from COVID-19 and Implications for the Social Security Administration. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 24, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Fungal Compound Sapinopyridione Shows Anti-SARS-CoV-2 Activity in Cells by October 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Fungal Compound Sapinopyridione Shows Anti-SARS-CoV-2 Activity in Cells Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A compound produced by an endophytic fungus isolated from Zanthoxylum piperitum shows potent activity against SARS-CoV-2 in infected cells, according to a study published in The Journal of Antibiotics on 23 October 2026. Shoji Maehara, Chiho Takahara, Ryo Watanabe, Serino Yoshitake, Toshiyuki Hata and colleagues, working with Shogo Nakajima, Hirofumi Ohashi and Koichi Watashi, isolated endophytic fungi from the plant and evaluated the anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity of their culture extracts. Of the 12 fungal isolates tested, six produced culture extracts that exhibited significant antiviral activity in SARS-CoV-2–infected cells. Three of these six active extracts also showed distinct inhibitory effects on the viral 3C-like (3CL) protease, indicating that the extracts act on a defined viral enzyme in addition to their broader antiviral activity in the cell-based assays. Chemical analysis of the active extracts identified sapinopyridione as the principal active metabolite. The compound is produced by a Botryosphaeria endophyte recovered from Zanthoxylum piperitum. In the infected-cell experiments, sapinopyridione displayed potent anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity, with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 2.45 μM, equivalent to 0.58 μg/mL. The researchers report that this potency makes the compound a notable candidate among the metabolites recovered from the fungal collection. The study was motivated by the observation that endophytic fungi produce secondary metabolites that protect their host plants from external threats, a symbiotic system the authors describe as a promising source of antiviral compounds. By screening culture extracts rather than individual purified molecules from the outset, the team could link antiviral activity in infected cells to specific fungal isolates and then narrow down the responsible metabolite through chemical analysis. The authors conclude that sapinopyridione derivatives are promising lead compounds for the development of antiviral agents targeting SARS-CoV-2. The findings rest on cell-culture experiments with a limited set of 12 isolates from a single plant species, so they do not establish efficacy in humans. content: COVID-19后疲劳的多因素生物标志物谱:持续性炎症、遗传变异与hs-CRP关联的一年纵向随访研究 《European Journal of Applied Physiology》:Multifactorial biomarker profiles in fatigued and non-fatigued post-COVID-19 patients: insights from a one-year follow-up 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月25日 来源:European Journal of Applied Physiology 2.9 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Original Article Open access 目的:比较SARS-CoV-2(严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2型,SARS-CoV-2)感染后疲劳组、非疲劳组和对照组之间的血液生物标志物;评估纵向生物标志物变化;并识别与COVID-19后疲劳相关的遗传关联和生物标志物。方法:该纵向观察研究对确诊SARS-CoV-2感染者随访一年,依据疲劳严重度量表(FSS)将其分为疲劳组(n = 27)和非疲劳组(n = 13),并与未感染对照队列(n = 27)进行横断面比较。于四个时间点采集血样,评估细胞因子、血液学和生化标志物、炎症指数及基质金属蛋白酶(MMP)。采用聚合酶链反应-限制性片段长度多态性(PCR-RFLP)对选定功能多态性进行基因分型。组间比较采用广义估计方程(GEE),遗传关联采用比值比(OR)和95%置信区间(CI)评估。结果:基线时,COVID-19后疲劳参与者的白细胞介素-6(IL-6)(2.70 vs. 1.68 pg/mL,p < 0.001)、白细胞介素-8(IL-8)(6.09 vs. 3.68 pg/mL,p = 0.024)和高敏C反应蛋白(hs-CRP)(6.61 vs. 1.06 mg/L,p < 0.001)高于对照组。随访期间,疲劳组IL-6(平均差[MD] 1.27 pg/mL,p = 0.009)、IL-8(MD 1.98 pg/mL,p = 0.017)和hs-CRP(MD 4.16 mg/L,p < 0.001)高于非疲劳组。在探索性基因型分析中,疲劳与COMT(儿茶酚-O-甲基转移酶,COMT)rs4680(OR 13.85,95% CI 2.74–69.91)、NR3C1(核受体亚家族3C成员1,NR3C1)rs41423247(OR 3.76,95% CI 1.04–13.69)和MMP9(基质金属蛋白酶9,MMP9)rs3918242(OR 0.20,95% CI 0.06–0.67)相关。hs-CRP与FSS评分显著相关(B = 0.12,95% CI 0.02–0.21;p = 0.014)。结论:COVID-19后疲劳与持续性炎症和遗传变异相关,支持多因素生物学基础,并强调hs-CRP作为潜在标志物需进一步验证。图形摘要:COVID-19后疲劳与持续性炎症和神经内分泌失调相关。遗传变异(COMT、NR3C1、MMP9)与疲劳相关,而hs-CRP成为严重程度的最强预测因素。 研究背景:COVID-19后疲劳是全球常见后遗症,患病率高,并影响就业、生活质量、功能状态和心理健康;既往流感、Ross River病毒、Coxiella burnetii和EBV感染后也可见疲劳综合征,但SARS-CoV-2因ACE2广泛表达和多系统受累可能造成更复杂后遗症。已有研究提示病毒感染后疲劳涉及细胞因子/趋化因子、炎症和心血管风险标志物、血细胞参数、血小板、血液学炎症指数、MMP、脂质代谢、肝肾功能及肌肉功能和损伤等多领域改变;但COVID-19后疲劳与非疲劳者之间这些标志物模式差异、是否持续一年、遗传变异贡献仍不清楚。因此,研究人员比较三组血液标志物、纵向变化、遗传关联及与疲劳最相关标志物,假设COVID-19后个体标志物谱不同于健康人,且疲劳者炎症、血液和生化改变更明显。 瑞孚迪自动化解决方案>> 领 取 研究人员开展为期一年纵向观察研究,随访确诊SARS-CoV-2感染者,按FSS分为疲劳和非疲劳,并与未感染对照横断面比较;结论为COVID-19后疲劳与持续炎症和遗传变异相关,支持多因素生物学基础,hs-CRP为需进一步验证的潜在标志物。意义在于从免疫炎症、组织重塑、神经内分泌和宿主遗传易感性整合解释疲劳,并提示常规可及指标可能用于随访和风险分层,但需验证。 关键技术方法:2021年8月至2023年8月招募COVID-19后队列(61例入组,40例完成四次评估:疲劳27、非疲劳13)和对照(36例符合,27例纳入);基因分型用残余血样53例(对照22、疲劳20、非疲劳11)。用FSS分层;在21–30、31–90、91–180、181–360天四时间点采血;流式细胞术微球阵列(CBA)测细胞因子,临床实验室测血液学、生化、炎症指数、脂质、肝肾和肌肉损伤指标,酶谱法测MMP;PCR-RFLP测多态性;超声和等长测力计测股四头肌厚度和膝伸肌力矩;用GEE、Tukey事后检验、线性回归及OR/95%CI分析。 研究结果: 社会人口学特征:GEE、卡方或Fisher检验显示组间年龄、性别、种族无差异;疲劳组教育程度低于对照,感染前体力活动少于对照和非疲劳组。 基线差异:GEE事后分析显示疲劳组较对照IL-6、IL-8、红细胞分布宽度(RDW)、hs-CRP、中性粒细胞、单核细胞、甘油三酯(TG)、γ-谷氨酰转移酶(GGT)、活性MMP-9、急性炎症状态指数(AISI)、系统性炎症反应指数(SIRI)更高,血红蛋白(Hb)、白细胞计数(WBC)、肌酸磷酸激酶(CPK)、股外侧肌和股内侧肌厚度更低;非疲劳组与对照无显著差异;疲劳组较非疲劳组活性MMP-9、GGT更高、股内侧肌厚度更低;血小板计数(PLT)、系统性免疫炎症指数(SII)、股直肌厚度有总体组间差异但事后无显著配对。 性别相关红细胞参数:COVID-19后参与者中男性红细胞计数(RBC)、Hb、血细胞比容(HCT)高于女性(p < 0.001)。 随访期间比较:细胞因子和趋化因子:GEE显示疲劳组IL-6和IL-8高于非疲劳组;其他细胞因子无差异,无组×时间交互。炎症和心血管风险标志物:疲劳组hs-CRP高于非疲劳组;同型半胱氨酸(Hcy)第二评估高于基线;RDW总体评估效应显著但事后未检出;无交互。红细胞参数:疲劳组平均红细胞血红蛋白量(MCH)、平均红细胞血红蛋白浓度(MCHC)低于非疲劳组;RBC、Hb、HCT有评估主效应,第三/四次RBC和HCT高于第二次,第四次Hb高于第一次且第三/四次高于第二次;无交互。白细胞参数:疲劳组中性粒细胞高于非疲劳组;单核细胞有组内差异但事后未检出;其他无差异。血小板:疲劳组PLT高于非疲劳组;平均血小板体积(MPV)无差异。血液学炎症指数:疲劳组AISI、SII高于非疲劳组;SIRI、AISI有组内差异但事后未显著;无交互。MMP:疲劳组活性和pro MMP-9高于非疲劳组;活性MMP-2有组内差异和组×时间交互;pro MMP-2无组间差异。脂质谱:TG有组×时间交互,第二评估疲劳组更高;其他血脂无差异。肝肾功能:无组间差异;碱性磷酸酶(ALP)和铁蛋白有组内差异,疲劳组第三评估铁蛋白低于第一;丙氨酸氨基转移酶(ALAT)和天冬氨酸氨基转移酶(ASAT)有组×时间交互。肌肉功能和损伤指标:疲劳组股直肌、股内侧肌、股外侧肌厚度和膝伸肌力矩更低;CPK有组内差异,第四评估更高;股外侧肌厚度有组×时间交互,疲劳组从第一到第二、第三增加,第四高于之前,非疲劳组第三高于第一。基因型分布和基因型-疲劳关联:疲劳与MMP9 rs3918242(OR = 0.20)、COMT rs4680(OR = 13.85)、NR3C1 rs41423247(OR = 3.76)相关;IL-8 rs4073趋势(OR = 3.33,p = 0.080);MMP2 rs2285053和FKBP5 rs7748266无关联。与COVID-19后疲劳相关的关键标志物:三个探索性线性回归模型比较AIC,含hs-CRP和CPK的模型3最优,解释23.1% FSS方差;hs-CRP为唯一显著预测因子(B = 0.12,95% CI 0.02–0.21,p = 0.014),CPK不显著。 讨论部分总结:COVID-19后疲劳患者炎症标志物较高,并存在部分血液生化、肌肉结构和功能差异及纵向差异;IL-6和IL-8升高与持续免疫激活一致,可能影响神经免疫信号和色氨酸-犬尿氨酸代谢。研究不能确定炎症先于感染或由持续病毒、免疫或组织过程引起;炎症、神经内分泌和遗传发现支持统一生物模型,遗传变异可能与疲劳状态而非感染本身相关,COVID-19可能是触发因素。COMT和NR3C1关联具生物学合理性,但基因分型不能证明多巴胺功能、糖皮质激素敏感性或下丘脑-垂体-肾上腺(HPA)轴失调;MMP9 rs3918242呈保护关联,IL-8 rs4073趋势具生物学合理性,所有遗传发现均属探索性。hs-CRP应视为候选相关指标而非临床预测因子;铁蛋白、Hb/HCT/MCH/MCHC轻微改变后正常,PLT和中性粒细胞持续升高,SII、SIRI、AISI持续升高;GGT升高提示氧化应激和亚临床组织应激;MMP-9升高提示细胞外基质重塑和炎症;肌肉厚度和力量下降、CPK低提示结构与功能损害但非诊断肌少症或无力症;股外侧肌厚度持续低可能与慢性低度炎症、线粒体功能障碍、氧化代谢受损和肌肉修复改变有关;TG高与长COVID和心血管风险相关;多项指标来自常规检测,具随访和风险分层潜力。局限性包括对照仅评估一次、样本小、无先验样本量计算、纵向测量受混杂影响、多结局和单核苷酸多态性增加偶然发现风险、遗传和回归分析缺乏外部重复,结果应视为探索性。 研究结论翻译:综上,研究结果支持COVID-19后疲劳的多因素模型,涉及免疫失调、组织重塑和宿主遗传变异。疲劳与COMT、NR3C1和MMP9变异相关,并伴随生化、炎症和肌肉相关改变。hs-CRP和血液学指数等可及指标可能有助于识别相关生物学特征,但临床使用前需验证。需要更大、更多样的机制研究确认这些关联并阐明因果通路。 研究背景:COVID-19后疲劳是全球常见后遗症,患病率高,并影响就业、生活质量、功能状态和心理健康;既往流感、Ross River病毒、Coxiella burnetii和EBV感染后也可见疲劳综合征,但SARS-CoV-2因ACE2广泛表达和多系统受累可能造成更复杂后遗症。已有研究提示病毒感染后疲劳涉及细胞因子/趋化因子、炎症和心血管风险标志物、血细胞参数、血小板、血液学炎症指数、MMP、脂质代谢、肝肾功能及肌肉功能和损伤等多领域改变;但COVID-19后疲劳与非疲劳者之间这些标志物模式差异、是否持续一年、遗传变异贡献仍不清楚。因此,研究人员比较三组血液标志物、纵向变化、遗传关联及与疲劳最相关标志物,假设COVID-19后个体标志物谱不同于健康人,且疲劳者炎症、血液和生化改变更明显。研究人员开展为期一年纵向观察研究,随访确诊SARS-CoV-2感染者,按FSS分为疲劳和非疲劳,并与未感染对照横断面比较;结论为COVID-19后疲劳与持续炎症和遗传变异相关,支持多因素生物学基础,hs-CRP为需进一步验证的潜在标志物。意义在于从免疫炎症、组织重塑、神经内分泌和宿主遗传易感性整合解释疲劳,并提示常规可及指标可能用于随访和风险分层,但需验证。关键技术方法:2021年8月至2023年8月招募COVID-19后队列(61例入组,40例完成四次评估:疲劳27、非疲劳13)和对照(36例符合,27例纳入);基因分型用残余血样53例(对照22、疲劳20、非疲劳11)。用FSS分层;在21–30、31–90、91–180、181–360天四时间点采血;流式细胞术微球阵列(CBA)测细胞因子,临床实验室测血液学、生化、炎症指数、脂质、肝肾和肌肉损伤指标,酶谱法测MMP;PCR-RFLP测多态性;超声和等长测力计测股四头肌厚度和膝伸肌力矩;用GEE、Tukey事后检验、线性回归及OR/95%CI分析。研究结果:社会人口学特征:GEE、卡方或Fisher检验显示组间年龄、性别、种族无差异;疲劳组教育程度低于对照,感染前体力活动少于对照和非疲劳组。基线差异:GEE事后分析显示疲劳组较对照IL-6、IL-8、红细胞分布宽度(RDW)、hs-CRP、中性粒细胞、单核细胞、甘油三酯(TG)、γ-谷氨酰转移酶(GGT)、活性MMP-9、急性炎症状态指数(AISI)、系统性炎症反应指数(SIRI)更高,血红蛋白(Hb)、白细胞计数(WBC)、肌酸磷酸激酶(CPK)、股外侧肌和股内侧肌厚度更低;非疲劳组与对照无显著差异;疲劳组较非疲劳组活性MMP-9、GGT更高、股内侧肌厚度更低;血小板计数(PLT)、系统性免疫炎症指数(SII)、股直肌厚度有总体组间差异但事后无显著配对。性别相关红细胞参数:COVID-19后参与者中男性红细胞计数(RBC)、Hb、血细胞比容(HCT)高于女性(p title: Deadline could be approaching to consider refund opportunities for COVID-19-related interest and penalties - EY
rss_summary_html: Deadline could be approaching to consider refund opportunities for COVID-19-related interest and penalties  EY
excerpt_original: Deadline could be approaching to consider refund opportunities for COVID-19-related interest and penalties EY
priority_tier_reason: 可信机构来源或已成功抓获正文
content_title: Deadline could be approaching to consider refund opportunities for COVID-19-related interest and penalties
content: Deadline could be approaching to consider refund opportunities for COVID-19-related interest and penalties Taxpayers that had interest and penalties imposed during the COVID-19 postponement period (January 20, 2020-July 10, 2023) likely have until July 10, 2026, to file protective refund claims or protective requests for abatement. Two courts held that IRC Section 7508A(d) creates a mandatory, self-executing postponement, disregarding the full disaster period plus 60 days and rejecting IRS regulatory limitations. The deadline for taxpayers to file protective refund claims or requests for abatements of interest and penalties imposed during the COVID-19 federally declared disaster period is likely July 10, 2026. Taxpayers should evaluate now whether they should file protective claims for refund or abatement. Background IRC Section 7508A(a) generally authorizes the IRS to postpone certain tax-related obligations for affected taxpayers for up to one year in connection with a federally declared disaster. The IRS primarily uses IRC Section 7508A(a) to extend filing due dates for taxpayers located in disaster areas. In 2019, Congress added IRC Section 7508A(d) to establish a mandatory, self-executing postponement period for tax-related obligations for "qualified taxpayers," beginning on the earliest incident date specified in the applicable disaster declaration and ending 60 days after the latest incident date. Congress, however, further revised IRC Section 7508A(d) in 2021 to substantially shorten the mandatory postponement period for disasters declared after November of 2021. The new subsection ties the end date to 60 days after the later of the earliest incident date or the date the declaration was issued. In Abdo v. Commissioner, 162 T.C. No. 7 (Apr. 2, 2024), a taxpayer filed a petition with the U.S. Tax Court 15 days after the window for filing would have originally closed. The Tax Court, however, held that the petition was timely because IRC Section 7508A automatically postponed the due date, making the original due date (March 2, 2020) fall within the postponement period. The Tax Court rejected portions of the regulations that attempted to limit the statute's mandatory postponement. In Kwong v. United States, 179 Fed. Cl. 382 (Nov. 25, 2025), the U.S. Court of Federal Claims held that IRC Section 7508A(d) requires the entire COVID-19 disaster incident period to be disregarded, plus 60 days — resulting in an automatic postponement period beginning January 20, 2020 and ending July 10, 2023. Therefore, a taxpayer's refund suit filed in early 2023 was timely even though the IRS denied the refund claim in late 2020. (The statute of limitations for initiating refund litigation normally expires two years after an IRS denial). Both courts in Abdo and Kwong applied the 2019 version of IRC Section 7508A(d) and declined to follow the IRS regulatory interpretations that would have imposed additional time limitations. Both courts also identified the resulting COVID-19 postponement period as January 20, 2020 through July 10, 2023 (i.e., 60 days after May 11, 2023). Specifically, the Court of Federal Claims held: "The plain meaning of that statute is that the automatic extension runs from the beginning of the disaster declaration, through the end of the declared disaster period, and until 60 days after the end of the declared disaster period." Deadline for protective refund claims or requests for abatement After Congress shortened the mandatory postponement period for disasters declared after November of 2021, taxpayers were confused about the deadline by which they had to file to claim a refund of interest and penalties that were imposed on late tax payments made during COVID-19. Consequently, many taxpayers likely assumed the deadline for filing refund claims had passed. With the holdings in these cases, taxpayers can likely now file for refund claims they previously had thought were time-barred. Implications Although Abdo and Kwong arose in procedural postures, their plain-text readings of IRC Section 7508A(d) could support taxpayers' challenge of interest, penalties, and recoverable refunds for certain periods during the COVID-19 postponement period (January 20, 2020 to July 10, 2023). The IRS's position and the ultimate resolution of these issues may continue to evolve through further litigation and administrative guidance. While the application of IRC Section 7508A continues to be reviewed, taxpayers should consider filing protective claims for refund or protective requests for abatement to preserve their rights. Particularly, IRC Section 7508A may apply to: Late-filing and late-payment penalties (e.g., IRC Sections 6651(a)(1) and 6651(a)(2)) computed by reference to due dates within the postponement period (e.g., IRC Sections 6651(a)(1) and 6651(a)(2)) computed by reference to due dates within the postponement period Estimated tax penalties (e.g., IRC Sections 6654 and 6655) when installment due dates fall within the postponement period (e.g., IRC Sections 6654 and 6655) when installment due dates fall within the postponement period Interest computations tied to postponed due dates (including underpayment interest and, depending on the facts, potentially overpayment interest computations) tied to postponed due dates (including underpayment interest and, depending on the facts, potentially overpayment interest computations) Information return penalties (including certain international information returns) when the relevant filing due date fell during the postponement period IRC Section 7508A also may extend due dates for certain refund claims. Taxpayers may wish to reassess whether the COVID-19 postponement period should be disregarded in applying refund-claim-limitation rules (including timing under IRC Section 6511 and related lookback limitations on the amount recoverable). Next steps Taxpayers that may have been assessed or paid interest or penalties during the COVID-19 postponement window, or may have refund positions affected by timeliness or lookback limitations, should consult with their tax advisors to determine what impact, if any, these developments may have on current positions, ongoing examinations, or potential refund/abatement claims. * * * * * * * * * * Contact Information For additional information concerning this Alert, please contact: Private Tax Services Dianne Mehany, EY Private National Tax Leader | dianne.mehany@ey.com Ashtyn Tarapchak | ashtyn.tarapchak@ey.com Tax Policy and Controversy Kiara Rankin, Americas Tax Policy leader | kiara.rankin@ey.com Published by NTD’s Tax Technical Knowledge Services group; Jennifer Mannetta, legal editor Document ID: 2026-1024

content_title: Castle Rock man gets federal prison time for COVID-19 loan fraud
content: By Lauren Penington | lpenington@denverpost.com | The Denver Post PUBLISHED: October 21, 2026 at 9:25 AM MDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... A Castle Rock man who took out millions in fraudulent loans against his bankrupt businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic will spend nearly two years in federal prison, federal officials announced Monday. U.S. District Judge Daniel Domenico sentenced Joshua Lybolt, 47, in July to 20 months in federal prison and ordered him to pay more than $5.3 million in restitution, according to a news release from the U.S. Attorney’s Office. Lybolt took a deal and pleaded guilty in March to one count of wire fraud and one count of money laundering, which dropped four additional counts of wire fraud and seven counts of money laundering from his case, federal court records show. Together, those two charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison, according to a copy of Lybolt’s plea agreement. The advised sentencing range in Lybolt’s plea agreement was roughly 4 to 5 years, but “the judge saw the complete picture,” said Todd Spodek, Lybolt’s attorney. “Your Honor’s ruling recognizes that this case was a complete anomaly in an otherwise honorable life,” Spodek said in a statement. “The Court recognized who Josh Lybolt was before this isolated chapter, who he has been since, and who he truly is at his core.” Between April 2020 and August 2022, Lybolt took out roughly $4.95 million in COVID-19 Economic Injury Disaster Loans and $41,667 from the Paycheck Protection Program, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. Lybolt previously owned businesses in Indiana and filed for bankruptcy before moving to Colorado, where he applied for those fraudulent loans on behalf of the bankrupt businesses, according to the release. His businesses — Prime Real Estate Corp., Broker Life, JMXE Capital and Lifstyl Real Estate — were not in operation on the dates required to receive COVID-19 funds. By declaring bankruptcy for those businesses, Lybolt discharged $5 million in debt, federal officials said. Instead of using the COVID-19 loans to make his creditors whole, Lybolt bought memberships in a country club and a luxury vacation club, four cars and property in Avon, Basalt and Snowmass Village, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. “The United States offered emergency financial assistance to Americans and businesses dealing with the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. But this defendant misdirected those funds for personal luxuries,” FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski said in a statement. content: Space Health Environment Humans Tech Nature Physics About Us Our Team Follow Us Big breakthroughs. Bold ideas. Straight to your inbox. Daily roundup Spark: Our top stories Does Pineapple belong on a burger? How Many People Have Died From Coronavirus? Explainer By ScienceAlert Staff (COVID-19 Dashboard by CSSE at JHU) Since its emergence at the end of 2019, the novel SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus has spread into the far corners of the world, taking the lives of young and old, rich and poor. At the end of March 2020, over 40,000 people had died from the virus. By early September, the total number of confirmed deaths worldwide from the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 exceeded 850,000. Exact numbers vary by a few thousand deaths, depending on the source. Tools such as those produced by Johns Hopkins University break down COVID-19 statistics on regular basis, which although precise, are only as accurate as the methods used to collect the data. Estimates calculated by bodies such as the World Health Organisation are typically based on tallying medical evaluations that link a positive SARS-CoV-2 test with complications believed to be responsible for a cause of death. Given limited testing capabilities around the world, underreporting and time lags of regional statistics, as well as the probability of complications going undiagnosed (especially early in the pandemic), the true count is likely to be much higher. How do we know when someone has died from COVID-19? The simple answer is we don't know for sure, though it's likely to be far higher than reported estimates. Unlike the 'manner of death', which distinguishes natural deaths like illness from suicide or homicide, a 'cause of death' ascribes a catalogued illness or chain of events to a person's loss of life. In many jurisdictions around the world, a cause of death is determined by a pathology expert, who assigns a code from the International Classification of Diseases to allow for easier reporting to international authorities. This might be straightforward in some cases where a patient with a positive blood result for SARS-CoV-2 has few (if any) pre-existing conditions. Among patients already dealing with illnesses such as cancer, asthma, diabetes, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the medical events leading to their death are likely to be more complicated. In such cases a pathology official would need to determine if the patient could have lived longer, were it not for the additional health impact of their coronavirus infection. How would we determine an accurate number of COVID-19 deaths? One method for estimating a more accurate total mortality for COVID-19 is to compare the total number of deaths for all causes during the pandemic with relevant statistics from a similar period in previous years. For example, by the end of July 2020, within a sample of 32 countries and 4 major cities, roughly 413,000 deaths were officially attributed to COVID-19. Statistics on death rates for those regions, however, found this period contained nearly 600,000 more deaths than typical for months corresponding to the pandemic. This implys nearly 200,000 deaths weren't being accounted for by the reports. How many of these might be 'missed' COVID-19 deaths is impossible to say. The pandemic has had other knock-on effects that impact health, such as interruptions to income and public services, reduced exercise, and reduced hospital admissions for conditions such as heart attacks. On the other hand, social distancing measures and improved hygiene has reduced the spread of other deadly illnesses. Finding a balance in the numbers will take time. It's possible we might never know exactly how many people would be alive if not for the global spread of SARS-CoV-2. In all likelihood, we are underestimating the number of people no longer alive as a consequence of the pandemic. The real death toll is likely to be far higher than the official one. Britannica Editors Last updated Oct. 22, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Top Questions What previous offices has Andrew Cuomo held? Andrew Cuomo served as secretary of Housing and Urban Development (1997–2001) under President Bill Clinton and as New York’s attorney general (2007–2010). He became governor of New York in 2011 but resigned in 2021 amid sexual misconduct allegations. In 2025 Cuomo announced that he was running for mayor of New York City. Is Andrew Cuomo married? Andrew Cuomo is not currently married. In 1990 he wed Kerry Kennedy, daughter of Ethel Kennedy and Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. The couple had three children before divorcing in 2005. That year Cuomo began dating TV chef Sandra Lee. The relationship ended in 2019. What is Andrew Cuomo doing now? Andrew Cuomo ran for mayor of New York City, but he was defeated in the primary by democratic socialist candidate Zohran Mamdani. News • Microsoft and Alphabet opt out of tokenized stocks in latest blow to ambitious plan from OKX and NYSE parent firm • Oct. 21, 2026, 1:08 PM ET (Fortune) Show less Andrew Cuomo (born December 6, 1957, New York, New York, U.S.) is an American politician and attorney who served as the governor of New York from 2011 to 2021, when he resigned amid sexual misconduct allegations. He previously served as secretary of Housing and Urban Development (HUD; 1997–2001) under Pres. Bill Clinton and as New York’s attorney general (2007–10). In 2025 Cuomo mounted an unsuccessful campaign for mayor of New York City. Early life and education As a teenager in Queens, New York, Cuomo put up posters to help his father, Democrat Mario Cuomo, campaign for state office. Andrew Cuomo graduated from Fordham University in 1979, the year in which his father became New York lieutenant governor. After graduating from Albany Law School (J.D., 1982), he ran the campaign that made his father governor (1983–95). For the next two years Andrew Cuomo worked as his father’s senior adviser in Albany. From assistant district attorney to secretary of HUD In 1984 Cuomo moved to New York City, where he became an assistant district attorney and a partner in the law firm of Blutrich, Falcone & Miller. During this time, he began to focus on the problems of the city’s homeless population, and in 1986 he founded Housing Enterprises for the Less Privileged (HELP), an organization that provided transitional housing for people living on the streets. He continued to advise his father from a distance and managed his successful 1986 gubernatorial reelection campaign. Discover the fascinating events that shaped the world, straight from our editors. SIGN UP Thank you for signing up! By clicking “Sign Up”, you consent to the Britannica Privacy Policy and Terms of Use. Cuomo’s efforts for the homeless led to his appointment in 1991 to chair the New York City Commission on the Homeless. After Clinton’s election as president in November 1992, Cuomo went to Washington, D.C., to help with the transition to the new administration and stayed to work on housing at the federal level. In May 1993 the U.S. Senate confirmed his appointment to HUD as assistant secretary for Community Planning and Development. Working closely with Vice Pres. Al Gore, Cuomo introduced new government policies to move the homeless into permanent housing with the help of transitional housing and expanded social services. In December 1996 President Clinton nominated Cuomo to become secretary of HUD, a post that he held from 1997 to 2001. Governor of New York Policies and COVID After losing his first New York gubernatorial bid in 2002, Cuomo won election as the state’s attorney general in 2006. He ran again for governor in 2010 and this time was successful in winning the office, handily defeating his Republican opponent, businessman Carl Paladino, in the general election. Cuomo was reelected to a second term in 2014. As governor of New York, he signed legislation in 2011 that legalized same-sex marriage in the state. In late 2014 he announced a ban on fracking, or hydraulic fracturing, citing a state-funded health study that found “significant public health risks” associated with the practice. He also oversaw tax cuts and an increase to the minimum wage. Cuomo faced controversy in 2014 when he abruptly closed a commission he had created the previous year to root out government corruption. Amid allegations that his administration had interfered with the panel, federal authorities conducted an investigation, and in 2016 it was announced that there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges. In March 2020 New York City became the epicenter of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, and Cuomo gained a national profile with his press briefings, in which he often criticized Pres. Donald Trump’s response to the crisis. The governor’s popularity rose as many praised his handling of the coronavirus outbreak, and he released American Crisis: Leadership Lessons from the COVID-19 Pandemic (2020). However, he was not without his critics, some of whom accused him of causing unnecessary deaths among nursing-home patients, a population especially hard-hit by COVID-19. Drawing particular criticism was a controversial state policy in which people infected with the virus were sent to nursing homes. Cuomo defended the plan, but in 2021 it was revealed that his administration had undercounted nursing-home deaths. The matter became the subject of an FBI investigation. Sexual misconduct allegations and resignation Another scandal emerged in late 2020 when a series of women began accusing Cuomo of sexual harassment. In addition, there were allegations that he created a toxic workplace. Cuomo denied the claims, and he defended his physical gestures as a way of “convey[ing] warmth, nothing more.” However, the state’s attorney general subsequently launched an investigation. The final report was released in August 2021, and Cuomo was found to have sexually harassed numerous women “through unwelcome and unwanted touching, as well as by making numerous offensive and sexually suggestive comments.” It also determined that his administration’s response to the accusations had contributed to “an overall hostile work environment.” Cuomo again denied any wrongdoing and accused the report of being biased. Calls for his resignation increased, including within his own party; notably, U.S. Pres. Joe Biden said that he should step down. Facing likely impeachment, Cuomo on August 10 announced his resignation, effective in two weeks. He left office on August 24 and was succeeded by Lieut. Gov. Kathy Hochul, who became New York’s first female governor. Explore Britannica Premium! The trusted destination for professionals, college students, and lifelong learners. SUBSCRIBE The scandal also ensnared his brother, Chris Cuomo, a TV journalist with CNN. Chris Cuomo offered strategic advice, and once that became public in late 2021, CNN fired him. Return to politics In 2023 there was speculation that Andrew Cuomo would be a candidate in the following year’s Senate race, trying to unseat Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat. Cuomo ultimately did not run, but in 2025 he officially entered New York City’s mayoral race. He was one of several candidates challenging the current mayor, Democrat Eric Adams, who was embroiled in a corruption scandal. Cuomo received endorsements from such notable figures as former president Bill Clinton, but he faced a strong challenge from Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist. The Democratic primary, which used ranked-choice voting, was held on June 23, 2025, and Mamdani topped the field by a comfortable margin. Cuomo, who finished second, conceded the race, but held open the possibility that he would contest the November general election as an independent. Personal life In 1990 Cuomo married Kerry Kennedy, daughter of Ethel Kennedy and Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. The couple had three children before divorcing in 2005. That year Cuomo began dating TV chef Sandra Lee. The relationship ended in 2019. Cuomo’s autobiography, All Things Possible: Setbacks and Success in Politics and Life, was published in 2014.
